# What this tool does

Clonal variety trials produce thousands of images. Each image is of a plant — a
specific genotype, at a specific location in a specific orchard block. For those
images to be useful, we need to know *which plant* each photo belongs to.

In the field, the photographer holds up a barcode or QR code card that
identifies the next subject (its genotype, plot location, or scion code) and
takes a photo of the card. They then take one or more photos of the plant
itself. The camera numbers these sequentially:
`IMG_0042.JPG`, `IMG_0043.JPG`, `IMG_0044.JPG`, …

**`kiwiDecoder` reads the identity-card photo and carries that identity forward
to all the plant photos that follow, automatically, across hundreds of folders
and thousands of images.**

The end result is a data table — one or more rows per image, each annotated with
the decoded identity. That table can then be used to link images to breeding
records, rename files by biomaterial name, or flag images where no identity
could be determined.

> **If you are reading this for an overview only:** §1–2 tell the full story in
> plain English. The rest of the document is a step-by-step guide for the
> person running the pipeline.

---

# How the identification works

## The photography sequence

Imagine the photographer moves through a block and photographs three plants:

| File | What was photographed | Has barcode? |
|---|---|:---:|
| `IMG_0041.JPG` | Identity card: code `SC00123` | ✓ |
| `IMG_0042.JPG` | Plant — shoot tip | |
| `IMG_0043.JPG` | Plant — leaf detail | |
| `IMG_0044.JPG` | Plant — whole canopy | |
| `IMG_0045.JPG` | Identity card: code `SC00456` | ✓ |
| `IMG_0046.JPG` | Plant — shoot tip | |
| `IMG_0047.JPG` | Plant — leaf detail | |

`IMG_0041` is the *donor* image — it provides the identity for every image that
follows, as long as the sequence numbers increase by exactly one. The moment the
sequence jumps (e.g. `0049` → `0052`), or a new barcode card appears, the chain
resets. Images with no barcode and no donor in their sequence are flagged as
`unknown` so they are never silently lost.

## What the decoded output looks like

After processing, the index CSV for this folder gains barcode and identity
columns. For the example above, the key columns look like this:

| file\_name | text | type | scion\_name | location\_address | prefix | number |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IMG\_0041.JPG | SC-001-ABC | scion | Hayward | TRC-17-13-19c | IMG | 41 |
| IMG\_0042.JPG | SC-001-ABC | scion | Hayward | TRC-17-13-19c | IMG | 42 |
| IMG\_0043.JPG | SC-001-ABC | scion | Hayward | TRC-17-13-19c | IMG | 43 |
| IMG\_0044.JPG | SC-001-ABC | scion | Hayward | TRC-17-13-19c | IMG | 44 |
| IMG\_0045.JPG | SC-002-XYZ | scion | Zesy002 | TRC-17-13-21a | IMG | 45 |
| IMG\_0046.JPG | SC-002-XYZ | scion | Zesy002 | TRC-17-13-21a | IMG | 46 |
| IMG\_0047.JPG | SC-002-XYZ | scion | Zesy002 | TRC-17-13-21a | IMG | 47 |

After all five pipeline steps the index CSV for each folder contains exactly
these columns:

| Column | Step added | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `dir` | Step 1 | Full path of the folder containing the image |
| `file_name` | Step 1 | Image filename (e.g. `IMG_0042.JPG`) |
| `ext` | Step 1 | Lowercased file extension (`jpg`, `png`, `heic`, …) |
| `full_path` | Step 1 | Absolute path to the image file |
| `index` | Step 2 | Symbol index within the image (1, 2, … if multiple barcodes); `NA` if nothing decoded |
| `code_format` | Step 2 | Barcode format decoded (e.g. `PDF417`, `QRCode`); `"unknown"` when the image was processed but no barcode was readable |
| `text` | Step 2 | Raw decoded barcode text; `NA` if nothing decoded |
| `type` | Step 2 | Code classification: `scion`, `location`, `plant-genotype`, …; `NA` if nothing decoded |
| `decode_status` | Step 2 | How the barcode information was obtained — see table below |
| `donor_file` | Step 2 | Filename of the card image whose barcode was propagated to this row; `NA` unless `decode_status == "propagated"` |
| `scion_name` | Step 3 | Human-readable scion name from KiwiCloud (e.g. `Hayward`) |
| `scion_genotype` | Step 3 | Genotype string from KiwiCloud (e.g. `K17.0004.03072`) |
| `location_name` | Step 3 | Site/trial name (e.g. `Te Puke Research Centre`) |
| `location_address` | Step 3 | Precise vine address (e.g. `TRC-17-13-19c`) |
| `file_owner` | Step 4 | Windows file owner — best proxy for the photographer |
| `camera_make` | Step 4 | Camera manufacturer from EXIF (e.g. `Apple`) |
| `camera_model` | Step 4 | Camera model from EXIF (e.g. `iPhone 13`) |
| `GPSLatitude` | Step 4 | GPS latitude in decimal degrees (if location services were on) |
| `GPSLongitude` | Step 4 | GPS longitude in decimal degrees |
| `DateTimeOriginal` | Step 4 | Capture date and time from EXIF |

**`decode_status` values:**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"decoded"` | The barcode was read directly from this image |
| `"propagated"` | The barcode text was copied from an adjacent card image (same prefix, sequential number). The source image is in `donor_file`. Treat as indicative — review `donor_file` if precision is needed |
| `"undecodable"` | This image was processed but no barcode could be decoded, and it had no valid donor to inherit from |

The biomaterial lookup columns (`scion_name` through `location_address`) are
only populated when a live database connection is supplied — see §4.3.

If a card holds multiple symbols (e.g. both a scion code and a location code),
each symbol becomes its own row, so a single image can produce two or more rows.

> **A note on M-prefix codes** (e.g. `M2126`, `MC079`): these are Clonal IDs
> for male parent genotypes, stored in the `genotype_synonyms` field in
> KiwiCloud rather than as primary biomaterial names. They are intentionally
> non-unique in the database (a single Clonal ID can map to multiple records).
> The pipeline will decode and carry the text forward correctly, but the
> `scion_name` lookup will not return a match for these codes.

## How decoded text is classified

The decoded text string from each barcode is automatically labelled:

| Decoded text | Type assigned |
|---|---|
| Starts with `SC` | `scion` |
| Starts with `RS` | `plant-genotype` |
| Starts with a letter then two digits (e.g. `A07`) | `location` |
| Anything else non-empty | `scion-genotype` |
| Empty / unreadable | `NA` |

## Traceability guarantee

Every image always contributes at least one row to the output. The `decode_status`
column tells you how the barcode information for each row was obtained:

---

**`decode_status = "decoded"` — the barcode was read directly from this image.**

The decoder opened the image, found a barcode-shaped region, and successfully
decoded the text. This image becomes the *donor* for any images that follow it
in the same sequence. One row is produced for each unique symbol found; a card
carrying both a scion code and a location code will produce two rows.

---

**`decode_status = "propagated"` — the barcode was copied from a nearby card image.**

The decoder could not read a barcode from this image (either there is no card in
frame, or the card could not be decoded). However, the image *does* have a donor:
a previously decoded image from the same sequence, with a sequence number exactly
one less than this one.

The full set of barcode rows from the donor is copied here, with this image's
`file_name` substituted. `donor_file` records the filename of the donor image,
so you can go back and check it if you need to verify the identity.

---

**`decode_status = "undecodable"` — no barcode could be decoded and no donor is available.**

This is the case that often needs explaining. The image was processed — all five
decoder stages ran — but no barcode could be read. In addition, no prior decoded
image is available to inherit from.

**How does the programme know there is no donor?**

The programme walks through the images for a folder in filename-number order (e.g.
IMG_7988, IMG_7989, IMG_7990, …). As it goes, it keeps track of the most recently
decoded image — the current *donor* — for each filename prefix (e.g. `IMG`).

The donor is reset to "none" whenever the sequence is broken. A sequence break
occurs in any of three situations:

| Situation | Example | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| The sequence number jumps by more than 1 | IMG_7988 → IMG_7990, skipping 7989 | Something happened between these two images. Carrying the old identity across the gap would be unreliable |
| The filename prefix changes | IMG_7990 → DSC_0001 | A different camera or session. No basis for propagation |
| No decoded image has been seen yet | First image in the folder | There is simply no prior donor |

When a sequence break occurs AND the current image has no decodable barcode of
its own, the result is `decode_status = "undecodable"`. The row is still written
— with `code_format = "unknown"` as a machine marker and `text = NA` — so the
image is never silently lost from the record.

> **Example:** IMG_7988 has a barcode (`decode_status = "decoded"`, donor for
> the sequence). IMG_7989 and IMG_7990 have no card in frame; they both inherit
> from IMG_7988 (`decode_status = "propagated"`, `donor_file = "IMG_7988.HEIC"`).
> IMG_7992 has no card *and* is missing IMG_7991 in the sequence — that jump
> breaks the chain. Even though IMG_7988's identity might be correct, the
> programme cannot safely assume this, so IMG_7992 is marked `"undecodable"`
> rather than silently inheriting a possibly wrong identity.

---

**`decode_status = NA` — a decoding error occurred at the file level.**

Something went wrong before the barcode search even started: the file could not
be opened, a Python module was unavailable, or an unexpected error was raised.
All symbol fields are `NA`. These rows can be filtered with
`is.na(df$decode_status)`.

---

This means the row count in the output is always ≥ the number of images, and
no image can silently disappear from the record.

To query specific statuses after building the catalogue:

```r
library(readr)
df <- read_csv(file.path(image_root, "catalogue.csv"))

# Images where the identity was propagated (check donor_file to verify)
df[df$decode_status == "propagated", c("file_name", "donor_file", "text")]

# Images that could not be decoded at all
df[df$decode_status == "undecodable", c("file_name", "dir")]

# Any file-level errors
df[is.na(df$decode_status), c("file_name", "dir")]
```

---

# Setting up the decoding environment

This section explains the software components that `kiwiDecoder` depends on,
why each one is needed, and how to install them. It is written for someone
who is comfortable with R but has not used Python or image-processing tools
before.

## The software landscape — what is doing what

`kiwiDecoder` is an R package, but it calls out to three pieces of additional
software to do its work:

| Software | What it is | What kiwiDecoder uses it for | Do you need to install it? | Where to get it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Python** (with specific packages) | A second programming language | Reading and pre-processing images; running the barcode decoder | **Yes — one-time setup** | Install Miniconda (a lightweight Python installer) from [docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html](https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html); then use R to create the `kiwidecoder-py` environment and install the required packages (see §3.5) |
| **ImageMagick** | A standalone image-manipulation program | Cropping images into tiles; converting HEIC photos to PNG before decoding | **No — bundled automatically** | Comes packaged inside the `magick` R package. Running `install.packages("magick")` in R is all that is needed |
| **ExifTool** | A standalone metadata reader | Extracting camera information (date, GPS, camera model) from image files | **No — bundled automatically** | Comes packaged inside the `exifr` R package. Running `install.packages("exifr")` in R is all that is needed |

In summary: **only Python requires a manual installation step.** ImageMagick and
ExifTool are installed silently as part of their respective R packages and need
no attention from you.

You do not need to write any Python, use ImageMagick from the command line,
or interact with ExifTool directly. All three are called automatically by
`kiwiDecoder` behind the scenes once they are in place.

## Why Python as well as R?

R is excellent for data wrangling, statistics, and writing analysis pipelines.
Python is excellent for image processing and has mature libraries for tasks like
opening unusual image formats and running computer-vision algorithms. The
barcode-reading engine that `kiwiDecoder` uses — **ZXing-CPP** — has a Python
interface but no R interface. Rather than rewriting the entire barcode engine
in R, `kiwiDecoder` uses the `reticulate` R package to call Python code from
inside R. You install and use `kiwiDecoder` like any other R package; the
Python calls happen invisibly.

## Python packages needed

Three Python packages must be installed inside the `kiwidecoder-py` environment.
You install them once (see §3.5). After that you never need to think about them
again — `kiwiDecoder` loads them automatically every time it needs them.

| Package | What it is | Why it is needed |
|---|---|---|
| **Pillow** (also called PIL — Python Imaging Library) | Python's standard image-reading library | Opens image files so they can be passed to the barcode reader |
| **zxing-cpp** (pip install name: `zxing-cpp`; Python import name: `zxingcpp`) | Python wrapper around the ZXing-CPP barcode engine | The actual barcode and QR code reader |
| **pillow-heif** | A plugin that adds HEIC/HEIF support to Pillow | Lets Pillow open `.HEIC` photos from iPhones (see §3.8) |

**How the packages are loaded — and what you need to do**

Once installed, these packages are loaded automatically inside two `kiwiDecoder`
functions:

- **`detect_codes_all_zxing()`** — this is the core barcode-reading function.
  Every time it is called (directly or as part of the pipeline via
  `resolve_folder_sequence()`), it runs these lines internally:

  ```python
  # (This is Python, running invisibly inside R via reticulate)
  import PIL.Image        ← Pillow: opens the image file
  import pillow_heif      ← pillow-heif: registers HEIC support with Pillow
  import zxingcpp         ← zxingcpp: reads the barcode
  ```

- **`decode_hierarchical_zxing()`** — this is the five-stage hierarchical
  decoder that calls `detect_codes_all_zxing()` on each region. It also
  imports Pillow and pillow-heif directly for Stage 5 (the greyscale upscale
  pass).

You do **not** need to type `import`, `library()`, or any Python command
yourself. The imports happen inside the functions, invisibly, every time the
pipeline processes an image. The only action required from you is the one-time
installation described in §3.5 — after that, `kiwiDecoder` handles everything.

## What is a conda environment, and what is `kiwidecoder-py`?

When Python is used across different projects, a common problem arises: Project A
needs version 1.0 of a package, but Project B needs version 2.0, and the two
versions are incompatible. A **conda environment** solves this by creating an
isolated, self-contained installation of Python and its packages for each
project — they cannot interfere with each other.

Think of it like `renv` for R projects: each project has its own library of
packages pinned to specific versions, separate from every other project.

**`kiwidecoder-py`** is the name of the conda environment created specifically
for `kiwiDecoder`. It contains only the Python packages that `kiwiDecoder`
needs. The name is arbitrary — it could be called anything — but
`kiwidecoder-py` is the convention used throughout this vignette and in the
package defaults.

> **One-time setup:** You only need to create the conda environment once on a
> given computer. After that, `kiwiDecoder` finds and uses it automatically at
> the start of each R session.

## Creating the Python environment (one-time setup)

**Step 1 — Install Miniconda** (if not already installed)

Conda is the package manager used to create the environment. Miniconda is a
minimal version that is all you need. Download and install it from:
<https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html>

Accept all the default options during installation. Restart RStudio afterwards
so R can find the new installation.

**Step 2 — Create the environment and install Python packages**

The simplest way is to use the built-in setup function, which handles
everything automatically:

```r
library(kiwiDecoder)
setup_kiwidecoder_env()
```

This will:

1. Create the `kiwidecoder-py` conda environment (Python 3.11 by default)
2. Upgrade pip inside it to the latest version
3. Install `pillow`, `zxing-cpp`, and `pillow-heif`
4. Verify that all three can be imported correctly

If you prefer to run the steps manually, the equivalent commands are:

```r
reticulate::conda_create("kiwidecoder-py", python_version = "3.11")

python <- reticulate::conda_python(envname = "kiwidecoder-py")
system2(python, c("-m", "pip", "install", "--upgrade", "pip"))
system2(python, c("-m", "pip", "install", "pillow", "zxing-cpp", "pillow-heif"))
```

> **Note on the package name:** The barcode-reading package is installed from
> PyPI as `zxing-cpp` (with a hyphen) but imported inside Python as `zxingcpp`
> (no hyphen). This is a quirk of how the package is published — `kiwiDecoder`
> handles it transparently and you do not need to do anything differently.

**Step 3 — Verify the installation**

```r
reticulate::py_config()
```

This prints a summary of which Python is active and which packages it can find.
You should see `kiwidecoder-py` in the path and `pillow`, `zxing-cpp`, and
`pillow-heif` listed as available.

**What to do at the start of each R session**

Once the environment is created, you only need one line at the start of each
session before loading `kiwiDecoder`:

```r
reticulate::use_condaenv("kiwidecoder-py", required = TRUE)
library(kiwiDecoder)
```

You can add `use_condaenv(...)` to your `.Rprofile` so it runs automatically
every time R starts.

> **Troubleshooting — wrong Python:** If `reticulate` picks up the wrong Python
> environment (e.g. a system Python installation), add the `use_condaenv()` call
> before `library(kiwiDecoder)`. The `required = TRUE` argument means R will
> stop with an error rather than silently falling back to the wrong environment.

> **Troubleshooting — packages missing:** If `py_config()` shows `pillow`,
> `zxing-cpp`, or `pillow-heif` as not found, re-run `setup_kiwidecoder_env()`
> or the manual pip install commands in Step 2 above.

## ImageMagick — what it is and how it is installed

**ImageMagick** is a free, open-source image-processing program that has been
around since the 1990s. It can open, convert, resize, and crop almost any image
format imaginable. Think of it as a command-line version of Photoshop that
other programs can call automatically.

`kiwiDecoder` uses ImageMagick (via the R package `magick`) for two things:

1. **Converting HEIC files to PNG** — before decoding, each HEIC image is
   converted to a PNG file once. All subsequent processing works on that PNG,
   which is much faster to open. See §3.6 for details.
2. **Cropping tiles** — the hierarchical barcode decoder (§7) cuts the image
   into overlapping sections to search for small or off-centre barcodes.
   ImageMagick does the cropping.

**You do not need to install ImageMagick separately.** When you install the
`magick` R package, a copy of ImageMagick is bundled with it for Windows and
macOS. To install `magick`:

```r
install.packages("magick")
```

You can verify it is working:

```r
library(magick)
magick::magick_config()   # should print ImageMagick version and enabled features
```

The output should show `heic` listed under *Enabled features*, confirming that
ImageMagick can handle Apple's HEIC format.

## ExifTool — what it is and how it is used

Every digital photo contains hidden data recorded at the moment of capture —
the date and time, which camera model was used, the GPS coordinates if location
services were on, and many more fields. This hidden data is called **EXIF data**
(*Exchangeable Image File Format*). It is embedded inside the image file itself
and is invisible when you open the photo normally.

**ExifTool** is a free program, written by Phil Harvey, that reads and writes
EXIF data from image files. It understands hundreds of camera brands and image
formats, including HEIC.

`kiwiDecoder` uses ExifTool (via the R package `exifr`) in Step 4 of the
pipeline to extract the fields needed for the output table: `camera_make`,
`camera_model`, `DateTimeOriginal`, `GPSLatitude`, and `GPSLongitude`.

**You do not need to download or install ExifTool separately.** A copy of
ExifTool is bundled inside the `exifr` R package. Install `exifr` the usual way:

```r
install.packages("exifr")
```

**The search messages you will see**

The first time `kiwiDecoder` is loaded in a new R session, `exifr` searches for
ExifTool and prints a progress log like this:

```
Could not find ExifTool at any of the following locations: ...
Trying perl command: `perl`
Perl found at `perl`
ExifTool found at `perl` with args "C:/.../exifr/exiftool/exiftool.pl"
Using ExifTool version 12.22
```

**These messages are informational, not errors.** ExifTool was found and will
work correctly. The messages appear because `exifr` checks several locations
before finding the bundled copy. To suppress them so they do not appear again,
run this once interactively at the start of each session:

```r
exifr::configure_exiftool()
```

This tells `exifr` exactly where its bundled ExifTool lives, so the search is
skipped on the next load. You can add this line to your `.Rprofile` for
permanent suppression.

> **Perl?** ExifTool is written in Perl, which is a third programming language.
> You do not need to know anything about Perl — `exifr` manages this completely.
> Perl is almost certainly already installed on your Windows machine as part of
> R's own tool chain. The `Trying perl command` message simply confirms that Perl
> was found and ExifTool can run.

> **renv snapshot warning:** Running `renv::snapshot()` may print
> `Could not find perl at any of the following locations`. This is a known quirk
> of how `renv` checks packages: it runs `exifr`'s Perl-detection code, which
> looks in fixed Windows locations rather than the system PATH. It does not
> affect the pipeline — Perl is found correctly at runtime.

## HEIC/HEIF files (Apple iPhone photos)

### What HEIC is

If the trial photographs were taken on iPhones, most or all of the image files
will end in `.HEIC` (or `.heic`) rather than `.JPG`. **HEIC** stands for *High
Efficiency Image Container*. Apple introduced it as the default iPhone photo
format in 2017 (iOS 11).

HEIC uses a more advanced compression algorithm than JPEG — roughly half the
file size for the same visual quality. The downside is that the format is less
widely supported: JPEG has been the standard since the 1990s and every imaging
library understands it, but HEIC requires specific support to be added.

### Why HEIC causes extra work for the pipeline

The barcode decoder (ZXing-CPP) works on image data that has been opened and
decoded from the file. For JPEG and PNG files this is fast — the files are
simple and all major imaging libraries handle them natively. For HEIC, the
compression algorithm (HEVC, the same as used in H.265 video) is much more
computationally expensive to decompress.

Without optimisation, `kiwiDecoder` would need to decompress the HEIC file
three separate times — once for Stage 1 (full-image scan), once for Stages 2–4
(crop tiles), and once for Stage 5 (upscaled greyscale pass). On a typical
laptop this takes around 27 seconds just for Stage 1 alone.

### How kiwiDecoder handles HEIC efficiently

`kiwiDecoder` avoids the repeated decompression by **converting each HEIC file
to a PNG once** at the start of processing, using ImageMagick. PNG (*Portable
Network Graphics*) is a lossless format — no image quality is lost — and it is
extremely fast to open. All five decoder stages then work on this temporary PNG
file instead of reopening the HEIC.

The temporary PNG is created in a system temp folder and automatically deleted
when the function finishes. It is never saved to your image folders and does not
appear in the output.

**Confirmed performance on a real iPhone 13 image (12 MP, 3 024 × 4 032 pixels
after rotation):**

| Operation | Time |
|---|---|
| Decompress HEIC directly (PIL) — Stage 1 old approach | 27.2 s |
| Convert HEIC → PNG once (ImageMagick) | 10.9 s |
| Open and scan the PNG — Stage 1 new approach | 1.3 s |
| **Time saved on Stage 1 alone** | **~15 s per image** |

Stages 2–5 also benefit, as they all read the same fast PNG. The one-time
conversion cost of 10.9 s is shared across all five stages, making the total
pipeline roughly twice as fast for HEIC images compared to the unoptimised
approach.

ImageMagick also automatically reads the EXIF orientation tag when converting —
if the phone stored the image sideways (which iPhones do internally), the PNG
is already correctly rotated so the barcode reader sees it the right way up.

If the HEIC → PNG conversion fails for any reason (e.g. the file is corrupted),
the pipeline falls back automatically to opening the original HEIC file directly
in each stage. No images are silently skipped.

### Which component reads HEIC at each step

| Step | What reads the file | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-conversion (once per image) | ImageMagick (via `magick`) | Bundled with the `magick` R package; handles HEIC natively |
| Stages 1–5 — barcode scanning | Pillow on the pre-converted PNG | PNG needs no special plugin |
| Step 4 — photo metadata | ExifTool (via `exifr`) | Reads EXIF from the original HEIC; bundled with `exifr` |

The `pillow-heif` Python plugin is also installed as a safety net: on computers
where ImageMagick's HEIC support is not enabled, `pillow-heif` allows Pillow
itself to open the original HEIC file directly. Installing both covers all
scenarios.

### Enabling HEIC in the file scanner

Add `"heic"` to the `extensions` argument of `scan_directories()` (it is
included in the default list):

```r
scan_directories(
  root       = image_root,
  extensions = c("jpg", "jpeg", "png", "heic"),
  ...
)
```

Extension matching is case-insensitive: `.HEIC` and `.heic` are both recognised.

### If your folders contain only JPG files

If trial photos were taken on a camera that produces JPEG files rather than
HEIC, simply omit `"heic"` from `extensions` and skip the `pillow-heif`
install. The pipeline works identically for JPEG files; all of the HEIC handling
described above is bypassed automatically.

```r
scan_directories(
  root       = image_root,
  extensions = c("jpg", "jpeg", "png"),
  ...
)
```

### What happens if `pillow-heif` is not installed

If you accidentally try to decode HEIC files without `pillow-heif` installed,
the pipeline degrades gracefully rather than crashing:

1. Step 1 (`scan_directories`) is unaffected — it only reads filenames, not
   image contents.
2. In Step 2, when the decoder tries to open each HEIC file, Pillow cannot
   recognise the format and raises an error. This error is caught quietly, and
   a single `NA` row is written for the image — the same output as a photo with
   no barcode.
3. Processing continues with the next image.

The result is `NA` barcode values for every HEIC file, with a warning message
printed for each one. You can identify the affected files, install `pillow-heif`,
and re-run Step 2 with `overwrite = TRUE` to decode them.

### Verified behaviour on real images

A full pipeline run was completed on a 10-image sample of iPhone 13 HEIC photos
from the `4 Ripe fruit photos (Auckland)/2026/` trial folder (12 MP,
captured 2026-02-16).

**Step 1 — `write_directory_index()`**

```
Rows indexed: 304
Extensions: heic (304)
Columns: dir, file_name, ext, full_path
```

All 304 HEIC files indexed correctly.

**Step 2 — `resolve_index_csv()` with KiwiCloud connection**

```
Decoding 10 image(s)...
Looking up biomaterial names for 1 unique code(s)...
Step 2 done in 482 sec
```

Nine of the ten images decoded to a scion barcode. The first image had no label
in frame and was marked `undecodable`. The decoded identity was propagated
forward automatically to the remaining eight images in sequence.

**Step 3 — `enrich_one_index_with_metadata()`**

```
file_owner:       10/10 non-missing
camera_make:      10/10 non-missing   (Apple)
camera_model:     10/10 non-missing   (iPhone 13)
GPSLatitude:       0/10 non-missing   ← Location Services was off on this occasion
DateTimeOriginal: 10/10 non-missing
```

All expected fields extracted from HEIC EXIF. GPS was absent because the
photographer had Location Services disabled at the time — this is a per-session
iOS setting, not a limitation of the HEIC format or ExifTool.

**Final output:** all 20 columns present across all 10 images, no errors, no
format-specific workarounds required.

# Connecting to KiwiCloud (Yugabyte)

## Why a database connection is needed

Barcodes and QR codes on field labels contain machine codes — strings like
`C.91606`, `SC-002-6MY`, or `RS022354`. These codes are the *key* into the
KiwiCloud database; they do not themselves tell you which variety the plant is,
where it is planted, or what trial it belongs to.

**KiwiCloud** is the KBC production database, hosted on Yugabyte (a
PostgreSQL-compatible cloud database). It holds the complete biomaterial
registry — every scion accession, cane, plant, and their orchard locations.
Without a connection to KiwiCloud, the pipeline can decode the barcode text but
cannot resolve it into a human-readable scion name or vine address.

**For image renaming, the connection is required.** The decoded barcode text
alone (`C.91606`, `SC-002-6MY`, etc.) is a machine key — not a human-readable
name. The columns needed to construct a meaningful filename —
`scion_name`, `scion_genotype`, `location_name`, `location_address` — are
only populated by the KiwiCloud lookup. Without them the catalogue is useful
for auditing which images carry barcodes, but you cannot produce renamed files
from it.

The connection *can* be skipped if your goal is purely to audit barcode
coverage (e.g. checking which images decoded vs. which are unlabelled),
because barcode decoding itself is entirely offline.

## Required R packages

Two packages are needed: `DBI` provides the database interface functions
(`dbConnect()`, `dbGetQuery()`, `dbDisconnect()`), while `RPostgres` provides
the PostgreSQL driver that `DBI` uses to communicate with Yugabyte.

```r
install.packages(c("DBI", "RPostgres"))
```

Both packages are already listed in `kiwiDecoder`'s `DESCRIPTION` under
`Imports`, so they are installed automatically when you install the package.

## Connection credentials

The credentials for the read-only KiwiCloud connection are stored in:

```
kbc/projects/stage-2/Data Science/data-validation/source/interact-with-yugabyte.R
```

The key parameters are:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Host | `a86e6e8c3e6f74590b0681a0128a39c3-76cf0d338a8ce628.elb.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com` |
| Port | `5433` |
| Database | `kup_obs_comp_prod` |
| User | `kup_ro` (read-only account) |
| SSL mode | `disable` |
| Password | see `interact-with-yugabyte.R` |

> **Do not put the password directly in a script that will be committed to
> version control.** Store it in your `.Renviron` file (see below) and
> retrieve it with `Sys.getenv()`.

## Storing the password securely

Add this line to your personal `.Renviron` file (one-time setup):

```r
# Open .Renviron in RStudio:
usethis::edit_r_environ()
```

In the file that opens, add:

```
YUGABYTE_PW=<password from interact-with-yugabyte.R>
```

Save and restart R. The password is now available in any R session without
appearing in your scripts.

## Opening a connection

```r
library(DBI)
library(RPostgres)

con <- dbConnect(
  Postgres(),
  host     = "a86e6e8c3e6f74590b0681a0128a39c3-76cf0d338a8ce628.elb.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com",
  port     = 5433,
  dbname   = "kup_obs_comp_prod",
  user     = "kup_ro",
  password = Sys.getenv("YUGABYTE_PW"),
  sslmode  = "disable"
)
```

Verify the connection is working before running the full pipeline:

```r
DBI::dbIsValid(con)          # should return TRUE
DBI::dbListTables(con)       # should list tables including export_biomaterial_wide
```

## Always disconnect when finished

```r
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

Leaving a connection open for hours can cause the server to drop it silently.
If you are running a long pipeline job, open the connection immediately before
the lookup step and disconnect as soon as it finishes.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `could not connect to server` | Not on the KBC network or VPN | Connect to VPN first |
| `password authentication failed` | Wrong password in `.Renviron` | Check `Sys.getenv("YUGABYTE_PW")` returns the right value |
| `SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly` | Long-idle connection timed out | Reconnect with `dbConnect(...)` and retry |
| `lookup_biomaterial_name() failed` printed as a warning | Connection dropped mid-run | Same — reconnect |
| Columns `scion_name` etc. all NA | Codes not found in database | Normal for M-prefix males and unregistered codes; check `lookup_biomaterial_name(code, con)` interactively |

---

# The pipeline — step by step

The full workflow has two steps, both designed to run on slow network drives and
both resumable if interrupted.

```
Step 1  scan_directories()
         ↓
  One CSV per folder: dir, file_name, ext, full_path
         ↓
Step 2  resolve_folder_sequence()
         ↓
  + index, code_format, text, type
  + resolve_log.csv
         ↓
Step 3  enrich_index_with_biomaterial(path, con)         [requires KiwiCloud]
         ↓
  + scion_name, scion_genotype, location_name, location_address
  (alternatively: pass con = to resolve_folder_sequence() at decode time)
         ↓
Step 4  enrich_index_with_metadata()
         ↓
  + file_owner, camera_make, camera_model,
    GPSLatitude, GPSLongitude, DateTimeOriginal
         ↓
Step 5  build_catalogue()
         ↓
  catalogue.csv in root — all 18 columns, all folders, one file
```

## Step 1 — Build a file index

Before decoding anything, `kiwiDecoder` builds a lightweight inventory of every
image file in the tree. This serves two purposes: it gives the decoder a stable,
ordered list to work through, and it means the slow recursive directory scan
happens only once.

```r
library(kiwiDecoder)

image_root <- "N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025"

scan_directories(
  root            = image_root,
  extensions      = c("jpg", "jpeg", "png", "heic"),  # HEIC requires pillow-heif
  prefixes        = c("^IMG_[0-9]{4}$", "^PMC_[0-9]{5}$"),
  checkpoint_file = "scan_checkpoint.rds",
  resume          = TRUE
)
```

**What it produces:** one CSV file per folder, e.g.
`Block_A/Block_A.csv`, containing four columns: `dir`, `file_name`, `ext`,
`full_path`. These become the input to Step 2.

**Key parameters:**

| Parameter | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `resume = TRUE` | Picks up where it left off if interrupted |
| `checkpoint_interval` | Save the RDS checkpoint every N folders (default 10). Higher values mean fewer writes on a slow network drive |
| `prefixes` | Regex patterns matched against the filename stem — images not matching any pattern are skipped |
| `dry_run = TRUE` | Scan without writing files — useful for checking what would be indexed |

**What you see while Step 1 runs:**

```
2026-06-02 12:51:32 | Step 1: scanning directories...
  |==                                                           |   2%
  |=======                                                      |  10%
  |==============                                               |  20%
  ...
```

There are two things that may look surprising:

1. **There is a delay before the progress bar appears.** Before the loop can
   start, `scan_directories()` calls `list.dirs()` to enumerate *every*
   directory in the entire tree. On a large collection stored on a network
   drive, this initial enumeration can take **5–15 minutes** with no visible
   output. The progress bar only appears once enumeration is complete and the
   loop begins. This is normal — just wait.

2. **CSV files do not appear for every tick of the bar.** The progress bar
   counts *all* directories in the tree, including intermediate parent folders
   (e.g. `1 Female Photos/`, `2021_22/`) that contain only subfolders and no
   image files directly. These scan instantly and produce no CSV. A CSV is
   written only when a folder **directly contains** image files with a matching
   extension. On a deeply nested collection the bar may advance past 20–30%
   before the first CSV appears — this is expected, not a sign that something
   is wrong.

The scan processes folders **alphabetically and depth-first**: it completes the
entire subtree under the first alphabetical subfolder before moving to the next.
So the first CSV written will be in the first alphabetical leaf folder that
contains images (e.g. `1 Female Photos/2020_21_or_older/2020_21_or_older.csv`).
Watch for that file in File Explorer to confirm the scan is writing correctly.

> **Running as a background job:** the progress bar renders correctly in
> RStudio's Background Jobs pane. However, it does not print a message for each
> individual folder — it simply advances as each directory is processed. This is
> by design: Step 1 is a file-system scan, not an image decoder, so the only
> useful progress signal is the bar itself. Run the pipeline via
> `source("scripts/launch_pipeline.R")` and watch the bar in the Background Jobs
> tab; CSV files will begin appearing in the image folders on N:/ once the scan
> reaches the first leaf folder containing images.

To index a single folder manually:

```r
write_directory_index(
  dir        = "N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/Block_A",
  extensions = c("jpg", "jpeg", "png", "heic"),   # default; omit heic if pillow-heif not installed
  csv_path   = "N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/Block_A/Block_A.csv"
)
```

## Step 2 — Decode barcodes and propagate identities

`resolve_folder_sequence()` reads every index CSV under `image_root`, decodes
each image, applies the sequence propagation described in §2, and writes the
enriched result back to the same CSV files.

```r
resolve_folder_sequence(path = image_root)
```

That is all that is needed for a standard run. Progress is logged continuously
to `resolve_log.csv` in `image_root`.

**What happens internally, for each index file:**

1. Reads the CSV
2. Decodes every image using hierarchical cropping (see §7)
3. Parses each filename into a prefix (`IMG`) and sequence number (`42`)
4. Tracks the most recently decoded image as the *donor* for that prefix
5. Propagates the donor's symbols forward to consecutive images (same prefix,
   number + 1)
6. Joins decoded symbols back to the index (one output row per symbol)
7. Writes the enriched CSV back to disk
8. Appends one row per image to `resolve_log.csv`

**To process a single folder** (for re-running one area or testing):

```r
resolve_index_csv("N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/Block_A/Block_A.csv")
```

## Step 3 — Look up plant identity in KiwiCloud (optional)

Once barcodes are decoded, each unique code is looked up in the KiwiCloud
database to retrieve the scion name, genotype, and orchard location. There
are two ways to do this:

For how to open a connection, see **§4 Connecting to KiwiCloud**. Once `con`
is a valid DBI connection object, pass it to the pipeline.

### Route A — at decode time (recommended when decoding from scratch)

Pass the connection to `resolve_folder_sequence()` and the lookup happens
automatically as part of decoding:

```r
con <- dbConnect(...)   # see §4

resolve_folder_sequence(path = image_root, con = con)

dbDisconnect(con)
```

### Route B — as a separate enrichment step (when CSVs are already decoded)

`enrich_index_with_biomaterial()` reads already-decoded CSVs and adds the
identity columns without re-decoding any images. Use this when:

- You decoded without a database connection and now want to add identity columns
- Database records have been updated and you want to refresh the lookup

```r
con <- dbConnect(...)   # see §4

enrich_index_with_biomaterial(path = image_root, con = con)

# For a single folder:
enrich_one_index_with_biomaterial(
  "N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/Block_A/Block_A.csv",
  con = con
)

dbDisconnect(con)
```

CSV files that already have a `scion_name` column are skipped by default.
Use `overwrite = TRUE` to re-query and replace the identity columns.

### What the lookup returns

The lookup handles three barcode types automatically:

| Barcode prefix | Type | Lookup strategy |
|---|---|---|
| `C.` (e.g. `C.91606`) | Cane | Finds the cane record, then joins to its scion via `cane_scion_id` |
| `SC-` (e.g. `SC-001-ABC`) | Scion | Direct match on `biomaterial_name` |
| `RS` (e.g. `RS022354`) | Plant | Direct match on `biomaterial_name` |
| Other text | Tries `biomaterial_name` then the `aliases` array | e.g. `T19.58-16-30a` appears only as an alias |

Codes not found in the database (including M-prefix male Clonal IDs — see §2.2)
will have `NA` for all identity columns.

To check a handful of codes interactively without processing a full folder:

```r
lookup_biomaterial_name(c("C.91606", "SC-002-6MY"), con)
```

## Speeding things up with parallel decoding

The image-decoding step is embarrassingly parallel — each image is decoded
independently. If you have the `furrr` and `future` packages installed, decoding
can use multiple CPU cores at once.

### How to check how many cores your machine has

Run this in R before deciding how many workers to use:

```r
parallel::detectCores()                  # logical cores  (includes hyperthreading)
parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)   # physical cores (the real compute units)
```

**What the numbers mean:**

Modern laptops and desktops use a technology called **hyperthreading** (Intel)
or **simultaneous multithreading** (AMD) that makes each physical core appear
as two logical cores to the operating system. For example, a 4-physical-core
laptop may report 8 logical cores.

- **Physical cores** are the actual independent compute units. For
  CPU-intensive work (heavy calculation), the physical core count is the
  ceiling on genuine parallelism.
- **Logical cores** (physical × 2 with hyperthreading) can still be useful
  even for intensive work if the task involves waiting — for example, reading
  image files from a network drive. While one worker waits for a file to
  arrive over the network, a second worker on the same physical core can be
  using the CPU to process the previous image. This *I/O overlap* means that
  going beyond the physical core count can improve throughput for network-drive
  workloads.

### How many workers to use

| Situation | Recommended `workers =` |
|---|---|
| Images on a local drive, CPU-bound work | `parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)` — physical cores only |
| Images on a **network drive** (e.g. `N:/`) | `parallel::detectCores() - 1L` — logical cores minus 1 (leaves one free for RStudio and Windows) |
| Laptop on battery / need machine to stay responsive | `max(1L, parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE) - 1L)` — one physical core free |

> **Never use `detectCores()` without subtracting at least 1.** Using every
> logical core leaves nothing for the operating system and can make your machine
> unresponsive during the run.

### Example

```r
library(future)
library(furrr)

# Check your machine first
parallel::detectCores()                 # e.g. 8 (logical)
parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)  # e.g. 4 (physical)

# For images on a network drive — use logical cores - 1
plan(multisession, workers = parallel::detectCores() - 1L)

resolve_folder_sequence(path = image_root)

plan(sequential)   # always restore when done
```

The propagation and file-writing steps remain sequential; only the decode loop
runs in parallel.

If `furrr` is not installed, `resolve_folder_sequence()` falls back silently to
sequential processing — no code changes are needed, but the `plan()` call is
then ignored.

> **Note on parallel warnings:** You may previously have seen messages of the
> form `UNRELIABLE VALUE: Future generated random numbers without specifying
> argument 'seed'`. These arose because `tempfile()` — used internally to
> create temporary image crops — generates random numbers, and `future`
> flagged these as potentially non-reproducible across workers. The underlying
> barcode results were never affected. This warning has been silenced by
> passing `seed = TRUE` to `furrr_options()`, which enables parallel-safe
> random number streams across workers.

## Step 4 — Enrich index files with photo metadata (optional)

`enrich_index_with_metadata()` reads every index CSV under `image_root`,
calls `extract_image_metadata()` on the images it references, and writes the
metadata columns back into the same CSV file — in the same way that
`resolve_folder_sequence()` writes barcode columns back.

```r
enrich_index_with_metadata(path = image_root)
```

The six columns it adds are:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `file_owner` | Windows file-system owner (best proxy for photographer) |
| `camera_make` | Camera manufacturer from EXIF (e.g. `Apple`) |
| `camera_model` | Camera model from EXIF (e.g. `iPhone 13`) |
| `GPSLatitude` | Latitude in decimal degrees (only if location services were on) |
| `GPSLongitude` | Longitude in decimal degrees |
| `DateTimeOriginal` | Capture date and time as recorded by the camera |

For each CSV it prints how many of the N images have a non-missing value for
each field, so you can immediately see whether GPS was recorded and whether
file ownership is informative.

If metadata columns are already present in a CSV (e.g. from a previous run),
the file is skipped. To re-extract and overwrite:

```r
enrich_index_with_metadata(path = image_root, overwrite = TRUE)
```

**To process a single folder:**

```r
enrich_one_index_with_metadata(
  "N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/Block_A/Block_A.csv"
)
```

**Using `extract_image_metadata()` directly** (returns a tibble, does not
write to disk — useful for interactive inspection):

```r
library(readr)
df_index <- read_csv("N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/Block_A/Block_A.csv")

meta <- extract_image_metadata(df_index)

# Coverage summary — how many images have each field?
meta$field_summary

# The metadata tibble itself
meta$data
```

**Why the photographer is hard to identify:**

iPhones and Android phones do not write the photographer's personal name into
EXIF. The fields that would hold this (`Artist`, `CameraOwnerName`) are blank
for phone cameras. The best available approach is:

1. `file_owner` — the Windows account that owns the file. If each photographer
   copies photos from their own phone under their own Windows login, this
   correctly attributes each image.
2. `camera_make` + `camera_model` — if different photographers used
   recognisably different phone models, these can be used as a grouping proxy.

If GPS was on, `GPSLatitude` / `GPSLongitude` can confirm the image was taken
at the expected trial site.

**How `file_owner` is extracted:**

On Windows, `file_owner` is retrieved using the `dir /Q` command, which
reports the file-system owner (e.g. `PFR\mike.currie`) for every file in a
folder. `kiwiDecoder` runs this command once per *folder* rather than once
per *file*, so the number of network round-trips equals the number of
subfolders — typically ~20 for a standard session — rather than the number
of images (~4,400). The domain prefix (e.g. `PFR\`) is stripped so the
column contains only the username (e.g. `mike.currie`).

On non-Windows systems `file_owner` is retrieved via `fs::file_info()` and
will be `NA` if the `fs` package is not installed.

## Step 5 — Build a root-level catalogue

Once all four enrichment steps are complete, `build_catalogue()` reads every
per-folder CSV and concatenates them into one file at the root of the image
tree. This is the single place a human or analyst needs to look to find any
image in the collection.

```r
build_catalogue(root = image_root)
```

This writes `catalogue.csv` to `image_root` and prints a coverage summary:

```
Reading 412 index CSV file(s)...
  412 folders | 35408 rows | 31204 decoded | 29817 with scion_name | 27455 with GPS
Writing catalogue to: N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/catalogue.csv
```

The catalogue is a flat table — one row per barcode symbol per image, with
all 18 columns. It is safe to open in Excel (rows ≤ ~35K are fine) or load
directly into R for analysis:

```r
library(readr)
catalogue <- read_csv(file.path(image_root, "catalogue.csv"))

# All images for a specific scion
catalogue[catalogue$scion_name == "SC-001-ABC", ]

# All images taken by a specific photographer
catalogue[catalogue$file_owner == "Kathy.Ruggiero", ]

# Coverage: how many images decoded vs. total
table(catalogue$code_format)
```

`catalogue.csv` is excluded from all pipeline steps — re-running Steps 1–4
will not read or overwrite it. Regenerate it by running `build_catalogue()`
again after any pipeline updates.

> **Note:** the catalogue is a snapshot. If new images are added and processed,
> run `build_catalogue()` again to refresh it.

---

# Monitoring a long run

Decoding large image collections can take hours. `kiwiDecoder` writes a
per-image log as it goes, so you can check progress at any time without
interrupting the job.

## Checking progress interactively

```r
monitor_resolve_progress(root = image_root)
```

This prints:

- how many images have been processed
- estimated total and percentage complete
- the most recently decoded filename
- a tail of the last 10 log entries

## Running a live monitor in parallel

The recommended approach is to run the decoder in the background and watch
progress in an RStudio Job — two separate R sessions, neither blocking the
other.

**In your main console — start the background decoder:**

```r
library(callr)

bg <- r_bg(
  func = function(root) {
    library(kiwiDecoder)
    resolve_folder_sequence(root)
  },
  args = list(root = image_root)
)
```

**Save this as `scripts/monitor_resolve.R` and run it as an RStudio Local Job**
(*Jobs* pane → *Start Local Job*):

```r
root <- "N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025"

repeat {
  cat("Refreshed:", format(Sys.time()), "\n")
  kiwiDecoder::monitor_resolve_progress(root)
  Sys.sleep(10)
}
```

The monitor refreshes every 10 seconds in its own panel and survives console
resets. When the background job finishes:

```r
bg$is_alive()    # FALSE when done
bg$get_result()  # retrieve the output
```

## The log file

`resolve_log.csv` (written to `image_root`) has one row per image processed:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `time` | Timestamp when the image was processed |
| `csv_file` | Path to the index CSV being processed |
| `image_file` | Filename (e.g. `IMG_0042.JPG`) |
| `full_path` | Full path to the image on disk |
| `prefix` | Parsed filename prefix (e.g. `IMG`) |
| `number` | Parsed sequence number (e.g. `42`) |
| `decoded` | `TRUE` if at least one barcode was successfully read |

---

# How decoding works inside

## The barcode engine

For each image, `kiwiDecoder` calls:

- **Pillow** (Python Imaging Library) to open the image file.
  JPEG, PNG, and TIFF are supported natively. **HEIC/HEIF** requires the
  `pillow-heif` plugin, which is registered automatically before every image
  open — see *"HEIC/HEIF files"* in §3 for setup details.
- **ZXing-CPP** to scan for and decode symbols

Supported barcode formats include QR Code, PDF417, Data Matrix, Code 128,
Code 39, and most other common standards.

## Hierarchical cropping

Many barcode cards are photographed at an angle, in partial shade, or occupy
only a corner of the frame. To maximise detection — and to find **all** barcodes
when an image contains more than one — `decode_hierarchical_zxing()` runs all
five stages and accumulates every unique barcode it finds:

1. **Full image** — the fast path; finds most large, prominent barcodes in a
   single pass.
2. **Top half / bottom half** — catches barcodes confined to one end of the
   frame.
3. **Top third / middle third / bottom third** — horizontal bands for barcodes
   in the middle of a tall image.
4. **Sliding-window grid with 50 % overlap** — approximately 25 tiles covering
   the whole image. The overlap ensures that no small barcode is split across
   a tile boundary. For images carrying up to 6 barcodes spread across the
   frame, the grid tiles each return all symbols they contain, so the full set
   is accumulated across tiles.
5. **Grayscale + autocontrast + 2× upscale** — covers barcodes that ZXing can
   locate but cannot pass checksum at native resolution. Upscaling gives the
   decoder more pixels per module, recovering barcodes on small printed-label
   stickers where individual modules would otherwise be too few pixels wide to
   read reliably.

Each stage is always run in full, regardless of whether earlier stages found
something. A barcode text seen at an earlier stage is not re-added if the same
text appears again at a later stage. The final `index` column numbers every
unique barcode 1, 2, 3, … in the order it was first discovered across all
stages.

This five-stage accumulator recovers many barcodes that a single full-image
pass would miss, including small embedded labels, high-resolution shots where
the barcode card occupies only a fraction of the frame, and identity cards
carrying multiple symbols (e.g. a scion code *and* a location code on the same
card).

## Diagnosing a specific image

If an image that should have decoded did not, these functions help identify why:

```r
# Raw ZXing diagnostics — shows what the decoder saw, including
# partial detections and checksum failures
debug_zxing_read("N:/path/to/IMG_0042.JPG")

# Try all crop regions and report which (if any) succeeded
decode_hierarchical_zxing("N:/path/to/IMG_0042.JPG")

# Simple single-image decode — returns one row per symbol found
detect_codes_all_zxing("N:/path/to/IMG_0042.JPG")
```

`debug_zxing_read()` is the most informative starting point: it shows the raw
output from ZXing including invalid candidates, error messages, and checksum
states, making it easier to understand why a particular image failed.

# Common decoding problems and how they are handled

## "No candidates" — barcode not located at all

ZXing reports zero candidates when its finder pattern detector cannot locate
any barcode-shaped region in the image at all. This is different from a
checksum failure: the decoder never even got to the bit-reading stage.

Common causes:

- The barcode card is out of frame, severely out of focus, or physically damaged
- The image is a plant photo with no card in frame (expected and normal)
- The barcode is printed on a small sticker label, and even after upscaling
  the module size is still too small for ZXing's finder heuristics
- Glare, shadow, or extreme angle across the barcode surface

**What the pipeline does:** if no candidate is found across all five decoder
stages, a single row is written with `text = NA`. If the image follows a decoded
card in sequence, it inherits that identity (`decode_status = "propagated"`).
If there is no donor, it is marked `decode_status = "undecodable"` — it is
never silently omitted from the output.

**What was attempted for stubbornly undecodable images:**

For images where a barcode is physically present but ZXing finds zero candidates,
the following preprocessing variants were tested systematically before concluding
the image is undecodable:

| Approach | Variants tested |
|---|---|
| Colour space | RGB (native), greyscale |
| Contrast | No preprocessing, autocontrast (PIL), histogram equalize (PIL) |
| Sharpening | Unsharp mask (radius 1, percent 200, threshold 3) |
| Upscaling | 1×, 2×, 3×, 4× (LANCZOS resampling) |
| Region | Full image, centre-third crop, full-width centre-strip |
| Rotation | 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° (in addition to EXIF auto-rotation) |

All combinations were applied to the same image with the same ZXing settings
(`try_rotate = TRUE`, `try_downscale = TRUE`). When every combination returns
zero candidates, the conclusion is that the image quality is below the threshold
at which ZXing's pattern finder can operate — no software-only fix is available
without substantially different source material.

> **Practical implication:** for images that reach `decode_status = "undecodable"`,
> the correct action depends on context. If the image is a plant photo (no card
> expected), the `"undecodable"` status simply records a sequence gap and the
> image still has its full metadata (EXIF, file owner, GPS if available). If the
> image *should* have had a readable card, the card itself likely needs to be
> rephotographed closer or in better light.

> **Potential future improvement:** OpenCV's CLAHE (Contrast Limited Adaptive
> Histogram Equalization) applies local contrast stretching that can recover
> barcodes in uneven lighting. Installing `opencv-python-headless` in the
> `kiwidecoder-py` conda environment and adding a CLAHE pass before Stage 5
> would be the most promising additional step to try for borderline images.
> This has not yet been implemented because OpenCV is not included in the
> base environment to keep the install footprint small.

## "ChecksumError" — barcode found, but bits corrupted

ZXing located the barcode and attempted to decode it, but the checksum did not
match — meaning the bit pattern was read incorrectly. This happens when:

- The barcode is a small printed-label sticker photographed on a high-resolution
  camera. Each barcode module (black or white square) occupies very few pixels,
  and ZXing's internal upscaling cannot recover enough detail to read every bit.
- The barcode is partially in shadow or has specular reflection.
- The image is slightly motion-blurred.

**What the pipeline does:** Stage 5 — the 2× upscale pass — is specifically
designed to recover these cases. The image is converted to grayscale,
autocontrast is applied to maximise bit contrast, and the image is upscaled
2× using Lanczos resampling. This doubles the pixel density per module and
allows ZXing to resolve the checksum correctly.

## Barcode near the edge of a crop boundary

The original non-overlapping 3×3 grid could split a barcode across two tiles,
with neither half containing enough of the symbol to decode. Stage 4 uses an
overlapping sliding-window grid with 50% step size (≈ 25 tiles), so every
point in the image is covered by at least two tiles and no barcode can fall
entirely in a gap.

## Sequence break — image with no barcode and no preceding card

If a photographer takes a photo of something else between card photos (e.g. a
close-up of fruit damage), the sequence break will be detected. The image is
labelled `code_format = "unknown"` and `decode_status = "undecodable"` rather
than inheriting from the previous card. This is intentional: the pipeline never
silently propagates an identity across a gap.

To find all undecodable images after processing:

```r
library(readr)
df <- read_csv(file.path(image_root, "catalogue.csv"))
df[df$decode_status == "undecodable", c("file_name", "dir", "decode_status")]
```

## Multiple barcodes on one card

If a card carries both a scion code and a location code, ZXing returns both
symbols. The pipeline produces one output row per symbol, so a single card
image will produce two rows, both propagated to all following plant photos.

## Identifying who took the photo

iPhones and most cameras do not write the photographer's personal name into
EXIF. See **§4.4 Step 4** for the full explanation of what `extract_image_metadata()`
extracts and how to use `file_owner` and `camera_make`/`camera_model` as
photographer proxies.

# Where output is stored

## Index CSV files

`scan_directories()` writes **one CSV per folder**, alongside the images it
describes. For example:

```
N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/
  Block_A/
    Block_A.csv          ← index of images in Block_A
    IMG_0041.JPG
    IMG_0042.JPG
    …
  Block_B/
    Block_B.csv
    …
```

### Why one CSV per folder?

This design was chosen deliberately for a collection of tens of thousands of
images stored on a slow network drive. The key trade-offs are:

| | One CSV per folder (this approach) | One monolithic root CSV |
|---|---|---|
| **Write speed** | Fast — each write touches only one folder's rows | Slow — every update reads and rewrites the entire file |
| **Network safety** | A failed write corrupts only one folder's CSV | A failed write on the N: drive could corrupt every image record |
| **Interrupted runs** | Natural checkpoints — finished folders are preserved on disk | Must track position manually; harder to resume |
| **Parallel workers** | Each worker owns its own file; no locking conflicts | Concurrent writes require coordination to avoid corruption |
| **Querying everything** | Requires `bind_rows` across many files at analysis time | Single read |

On a network drive with tens of thousands of images, the per-folder approach
means each write is small and fast, a network drop or interruption loses at
most one folder's work, and multiple workers can decode in parallel without
stepping on each other. The cost — reassembling all CSVs at analysis time — is
a one-line operation:

```r
library(fs)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

all_images <- fs::dir_ls(image_root, regexp = "\\.csv$", recurse = TRUE) |>
  purrr::map(readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows()
```

`resolve_folder_sequence()` and `resolve_index_csv()` **enrich these same
CSV files in place**, adding the decoded barcode and identity columns. The
original scan columns are preserved; the barcode and biomaterial columns are
appended.

## The decode log

`resolve_log.csv` is written to the root folder passed to
`resolve_folder_sequence()`. It is **appended**, not overwritten, so running
the decoder multiple times produces a complete history. Each row records one
image: the timestamp, which index file was being processed, the image filename,
and whether decoding succeeded.

## The scan checkpoint

`scan_checkpoint.rds` (written by `scan_directories()`) stores the list of
folders already scanned. It allows the scan to resume from where it left off
after an interruption. Once scanning is complete this file is not needed and
can be deleted.

## What happens when you re-run the pipeline

Every function in the pipeline is designed to be **safe to re-run** — either
on the same files (idempotency) or after new photos have been added to a folder
(incremental update). The table below summarises the behaviour of each step:

| Step | Re-run on same files | New files added to folder |
|---|---|---|
| `scan_directories()` | Skips already-scanned folders (checkpoint) | Rescan with `resume = FALSE` to pick up new files; index is merged safely |
| `write_directory_index()` | Detects no new files → returns unchanged | Appends new file rows; existing decoded columns are preserved |
| `resolve_folder_sequence()` | Detects all decoded → skips | Decodes only the new images; old decoded rows are kept intact |
| `enrich_index_with_biomaterial()` | All rows have scion_name → skips | Looks up only the rows with NA scion_name |
| `enrich_index_with_metadata()` | All rows have file_owner → skips | Extracts metadata only for rows with NA file_owner |

**No decoded data is ever overwritten on a re-run.** The default across every
function is `overwrite = FALSE`, which means:

- already-decoded images are left alone,
- already-enriched biomaterial rows are left alone,
- already-enriched metadata rows are left alone.

This is the safe default for production use. If you do need to force a full
re-run for a specific step (e.g. after improving the decoding algorithm, or
after database records have been updated), each function accepts
`overwrite = TRUE`:

```r
resolve_folder_sequence(path = image_root, overwrite = TRUE)          # re-decodes all images
enrich_index_with_biomaterial(path = image_root, con = con,
                              overwrite = TRUE)                         # re-queries all codes
enrich_index_with_metadata(path = image_root, overwrite = TRUE)       # re-extracts all EXIF
```

> **Warning — do not use `overwrite = TRUE` casually on the full image tree.**
> On the N: drive collection (35,000+ images at roughly 12 seconds per image),
> a full re-decode would take on the order of days. Use `overwrite = TRUE` on a
> single test folder first to confirm the result is what you expect:
>
> ```r
> resolve_index_csv("N:/Trials/.../Block_A/Block_A.csv", overwrite = TRUE)
> ```
>
> Then run the full tree only once you are satisfied.

### Picking up new files after a re-run

When photos are added to an already-scanned folder:

```r
# Option 1: delete the scan checkpoint and rescan everything
#   (write_directory_index() will merge new files without wiping old data)
file.remove("scan_checkpoint.rds")
scan_directories(root = image_root, resume = FALSE)

# Option 2: update just one folder directly
write_directory_index(
  dir      = "N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/Block_A",
  csv_path = "N:/Trials/Flower_buds/2025/Block_A/Block_A.csv"
)

# Then run the decode step — it will only process the new images
resolve_folder_sequence(path = image_root)
```

### If a run is interrupted

The pipeline is resumable at every step:

- **`scan_directories()`** — restart with `resume = TRUE` (the default). It
  reads `scan_checkpoint.rds` and skips folders already marked as done.
- **`resolve_folder_sequence()`** — restart without any changes. It checks for
  the `code_format` column in each CSV; folders already decoded are skipped
  and only the unfinished ones are processed.
- **`enrich_index_with_biomaterial()`** — restart without changes. Checks for
  `scion_name`; rows already enriched are left alone.
- **`enrich_index_with_metadata()`** — restart without changes. Checks for
  `file_owner`; rows already enriched are left alone.

In other words: once a step has finished writing to a CSV, that work is
permanent. Restarting the pipeline after an interruption costs only the time
for the work that was not yet completed.

## Summary of output files

| File | Written by | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `<folder>/<folder>.csv` | `scan_directories()` | Image index; enriched in-place by each subsequent pipeline step |
| `resolve_log.csv` | `resolve_folder_sequence()` | Per-image decode log, appended on each run |
| `scan_checkpoint.rds` | `scan_directories()` | Resume state for interrupted scans; can be deleted once scanning is complete |
| `catalogue.csv` | `build_catalogue()` | All per-folder CSVs concatenated into one root-level file |

All five pipeline steps write to the **same** per-folder CSV (Steps 1–4),
then `build_catalogue()` (Step 5) assembles the final consolidated view.
After all five steps the root directory contains `catalogue.csv` with all
18 columns across every image in the collection.
